headline: Double Creek Holds the Fluke, Weakfish Sneak In on the Dawn Tide
subhead: The bay's gone thick and warm, but the channel bends and the sedge banks are still paying off if you fish the right hour.
body_markdown:
Back when I was mating on the Point Pleasant party boats, there was an old-timer named Sal who used to say the bay in late July was like an old friend who'd stopped answering the phone — still there, still cares about you, just doesn't feel like talking during the day. I've thought about that line every summer since, and this week it's dead on. Barnegat Bay has slid into that heavy, syrupy stretch of the calendar where the shallows sit in the mid-70s by afternoon and the fish that made May and June so good have gone quiet, or gone deep, or gone nocturnal. Doesn't mean the bay's done with you. It just means you have to fish it on its terms now, not yours.

Fluke are the clearest example. A month ago you could drift the open flats off Tices Shoal and pick at keepers all morning. That bite has softened hard as the shallow water warmed past what these fish want to sit in during daylight. What's holding up is Double Creek Channel — the bends where the current stays honest and the bottom drops into that deeper, cooler stretch. I've been working the outside of the turns on the last two hours of the incoming, dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, and picking up keepers to five pounds along with plenty of shorts that make you work for your fish. Same story at the Barnegat Inlet-adjacent stretches — anywhere the current keeps moving is holding fish, and anywhere it goes slack and shallow has gone dead as a doornail by ten in the morning. If you're going to fluke this week, get out early, hit the channel structure, and don't waste your tide on the open flats.

Weakfish are the pleasant surprise. The back-channel bite that's been building statewide has found its way into our sedge banks, and I mean specifically the stretches south of Oyster Creek where the marsh drops off into deeper cuts. First light, before the sun's had a chance to punch through, has been the window — soft plastics, 4-inch chartreuse or pink Bass Assassins on a light jighead, worked slow along the channel edges. Nothing frantic about the retrieve. Let it sink, twitch it twice, let it sink again. These fish aren't chasing anything down right now, they're eating what drifts past them, so match that pace. I had two anglers out of Forked River last Tuesday morning who boated four weakfish in that 16-to-19-inch range before seven a.m., then nothing the rest of the day. That's the pattern — tight window, good fish, then it shuts like someone flipped a switch.

Bluefish are still the most reliable thing going, and if you want visible, aggressive action, that's your fish this week. Bunker pods are pushing in and out of the inlet with the tide, and the blues are riding right on top of them. I've watched them push bait against the Barnegat Light bulkheads and off the north end of Island Beach on the outgoing, and when that happens it doesn't matter what you throw — a Hopkins jig, a bunker spoon, a topwater popper — they'll eat it. We flagged this pattern last week, said the bluefish push would keep spreading along the coast as the bunker moved, and that's exactly what's playing out here, with fresh schools showing at the inlet mouth on nearly every tide change. Just watch your leader — 20-pound fluorocarbon minimum, because these fish are runing bigger than the usual summer cocktail blues and they'll cut you off on wire-light gear.

Striped bass are where the honesty has to come in. They've gone essentially nocturnal on us, same as the rest of the coast from here through southern New England. Daytime, they're holding deep on the channel structure and current seams around the inlet, refusing to show themselves except as the occasional sonar mark you can't tempt. We called this one too — said the pattern would hold as long as the warm, stable weather stuck around, and it has, day after day of calm and heat with nothing to break the thermal stack. If you want bass, you're fishing after dark now — eels drifted on the current seams inside the inlet, or bunker chunks fished on the bottom around the deeper bends of Double Creek. I put a client on two schoolies and one 27-incher last Thursday night working chunk bait off the rocks near the inlet on the last of the ebb. Slow fishing, but real fishing, and the kind of thing that rewards patience over volume.

Crabbing, for what it's worth, is about the easiest thing going right now — the heat that's shutting down the daytime bite is exactly what the blue claws want, and the back creeks are thick with them. If the fishing's slow, that's not a bad way to spend an afternoon with the kids.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break unless we get some wind and a real tide-flushing event to knock the shallow water down a few degrees. If the calm holds through the weekend, I'd keep doing what's working — early mornings on the weakfish at the sedges, fluke worked deep in Double Creek on the moving tide, bluefish whenever you see bait get pushed around the inlet, and stripers strictly after dark. If we get a blow out of the northeast that stirs things up, watch for the fluke bite to wake back up on the flats for a day or two after — that's happened before, and it's worth checking Tices Shoal again if the weather turns.
